proofs.proof_tex:
By \(\textnormal{ass:supply-range}\) and \(\textnormal{def:uniform-dosage}\),
\[
 0<u=\min\{L/p,1/2\}\le \frac12<1,
\]
so \(d^\star=u\mathbf 1_p\) is an interior dosage.  In particular, the positive-definiteness conclusion of \(\textnormal{lem:trace-identity}\) applies to \(\Sigma_k(d^\star)\).

We make the triangular change of basis explicit.  Put
\[
 m=2u-1,
 \qquad
 s=\sqrt{4u(1-u)}>0,
 \qquad
 g_i(x_i)=\frac{x_i-m}{s},
 \qquad
 \psi_T(x)=\prod_{i\in T}g_i(x_i)
 \quad(T\in\mathcal I_k).
\]
Under the product randomization at \(d^\star\), the coordinates \(X_i\) are independent and satisfy
\[
 \mathbb E_{d^\star}X_i=m,
 \qquad
 \mathbb E_{d^\star}(X_i-m)^2=s^2.
\]
Consequently \(\mathbb E_{d^\star}g_i(X_i)=0\) and \(\mathbb E_{d^\star}g_i(X_i)^2=1\).  Independence then gives, for \(T,U\in\mathcal I_k\),
\[
 \mathbb E_{d^\star}\{\psi_T(X)\psi_U(X)\}
 =\prod_{i\in T\cap U}\mathbb E_{d^\star}g_i(X_i)^2
   \prod_{i\in T\mathbin\triangle U}\mathbb E_{d^\star}g_i(X_i)
 =\mathbf 1\{T=U\}.
\]

For each \(T\in\mathcal I_k\), expansion of the product yields
\[
 \psi_T(x)
 =s^{-|T|}\prod_{i\in T}(x_i-m)
 =s^{-|T|}\sum_{R\subseteq T}(-m)^{|T\setminus R|}\phi_R(x).
\]
Because \(R\subseteq T\) implies \(R\in\mathcal I_k\), this defines a square matrix \(A\), indexed by \(\mathcal I_k\), such that \(\psi(x)=A\phi(x)\).  Ordering subsets by nondecreasing cardinality makes \(A\) triangular, and its diagonal entry indexed by \(T\) is \(s^{-|T|}>0\); hence \(A\) is invertible.  The preceding orthonormality calculation and the definition of \(\Sigma_k\) give
\[
 I_q
 =\mathbb E_{d^\star}\{\psi(X)\psi(X)^{\mathsf T}\}
 =A\Sigma_k(d^\star)A^{\mathsf T}.
\]
Therefore
\[
 \Sigma_k(d^\star)^{-1}=A^{\mathsf T}A,
\]
and, for every \(x\in\{-1,1\}^p\),
\[
 \phi(x)^{\mathsf T}\Sigma_k(d^\star)^{-1}\phi(x)
 =\|A\phi(x)\|_2^2
 =\sum_{T\in\mathcal I_k}\psi_T(x)^2.
\]

For each coordinate, direct substitution gives
\[
 g_i(x_i)^2
 =\begin{cases}
 \dfrac{1-u}{u},&x_i=1,\\[6pt]
 \dfrac{u}{1-u},&x_i=-1.
 \end{cases}
\]
Since \(0<u\le1/2\),
\[
 \frac{u}{1-u}\le\frac{1-u}{u}.
\]
Every term \(\psi_T(x)^2=\prod_{i\in T}g_i(x_i)^2\) is a product of nonnegative coordinate factors.  Thus all terms in their sum are simultaneously maximized at \(x=\mathbf 1_p\).  By \(\textnormal{def:maximum-leverage}\),
\[
 \mu^\star
 =\sum_{T\in\mathcal I_k}\prod_{i\in T}\frac{1-u}{u}
 =\sum_{j=0}^{k}\binom pj\left(\frac{1-u}{u}\right)^j,
\]
where the last equality groups subsets by cardinality.  This proves the asserted exact maximum.

Write \(\Sigma=\Sigma_k(d^\star)\) and define the proof-intermediate whitened rows \(w_a=\Sigma^{-1/2}x_a\).  Since \(0<u\le1/2\), the vector \(d^\star\) lies in \((0,1)^p\), so \(\textnormal{lem:trace-identity}\) proves that \(\Sigma\) is positive definite and the whitening is well defined.  Product randomization across units and the definition of \(\Sigma\) give independence of \(w_1,\ldots,w_n\) and
\[
 \mathbb E_{d^\star}[w_aw_a^{\mathsf T}]
 =\Sigma^{-1/2}\mathbb E_{d^\star}[x_ax_a^{\mathsf T}]\Sigma^{-1/2}
 =I_q.
\]
The exact-leverage proposition and the finite Boolean support imply, almost surely,
\[
 \lambda_{\max}(w_aw_a^{\mathsf T})
 =\|w_a\|_2^2
 =x_a^{\mathsf T}\Sigma^{-1}x_a
 \le\mu^\star. \tag{1}
\]

Apply \(\textnormal{lem:tropp-matrix-chernoff}\) to \(K_a=w_aw_a^{\mathsf T}\).  These matrices are independent and positive semidefinite, equation \((1)\) supplies \(R=\mu^\star>0\), and
\[
 \sum_{a=1}^n\mathbb E K_a=nI_q,
 \qquad
 \mu_{\min}=\mu_{\max}=n.
\]
For \(0\le t\le1/2\), put
\[
 h_+(t)=(1+t)\log(1+t)-t,
 \qquad
 h_-(t)=t+(1-t)\log(1-t).
\]
Both functions and their first derivatives vanish at zero, while
\[
 h_+''(t)=\frac{1}{1+t}\ge\frac23,
 \qquad
 h_-''(t)=\frac{1}{1-t}\ge1.
\]
Integrating twice from zero yields \(h_+(t)\ge t^2/3\) and \(h_-(t)\ge t^2/2\ge t^2/3\).  The two Chernoff bounds therefore give
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \mathbb P\!\left\{\lambda_{\min}\!\left(\frac1n\sum_{a=1}^nK_a\right)
 \le1-\varepsilon\right\}
 &\le q\exp\!\left\{-\frac{n\varepsilon^2}{3\mu^\star}\right\},\\
 \mathbb P\!\left\{\lambda_{\max}\!\left(\frac1n\sum_{a=1}^nK_a\right)
 \ge1+\varepsilon\right\}
 &\le q\exp\!\left\{-\frac{n\varepsilon^2}{3\mu^\star}\right\}.
\end{aligned} \tag{2}
\]
Moreover,
\[
 \frac1n\sum_{a=1}^nK_a
 =\Sigma^{-1/2}(F^{\mathsf T}F/n)\Sigma^{-1/2}
 =I_q+H_n(\varepsilon).
\]
For a symmetric matrix, failure of \(\|H_n(\varepsilon)\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le\varepsilon\) entails at least one of the two weak tail events in \((2)\).  The union bound and the elementary bound on a probability therefore prove
\[
 b_{n,\varepsilon}
 \le\min\!\left\{1,2q\exp\!\left(-\frac{n\varepsilon^2}{3\mu^\star}\right)\right\}
 =\min\{1,\delta_{n,\varepsilon}\}.
\]

On \(G_n(\varepsilon)\), the definition of the operator norm and congruence by \(\Sigma^{1/2}\) give
\[
 (1-\varepsilon)\Sigma
 \preceq F^{\mathsf T}F/n
 \preceq(1+\varepsilon)\Sigma. \tag{3}
\]
Because \(0<\varepsilon<1/2\) and \(\Sigma\) is positive definite, equation \((3)\) makes \(F^{\mathsf T}F\) positive definite on this event.  Inversion reverses Loewner order, so
\[
 \frac{1}{n(1+\varepsilon)}\Sigma^{-1}
 \preceq(F^{\mathsf T}F)^{-1}
 \preceq\frac{1}{n(1-\varepsilon)}\Sigma^{-1}. \tag{4}
\]
For every realization of \(F\) in \(G_n(\varepsilon)\), linear response and the estimator definition yield
\[
 \widehat\beta_\varepsilon-\beta
 =(F^{\mathsf T}F)^{-1}F^{\mathsf T}\epsilon.
\]
Conditional centering gives zero conditional mean, and conditional homoskedasticity gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \operatorname{Cov}(\widehat\beta_\varepsilon\mid F)
 &=(F^{\mathsf T}F)^{-1}F^{\mathsf T}
   (\sigma^2I_n)F(F^{\mathsf T}F)^{-1}\\
 &=\sigma^2(F^{\mathsf T}F)^{-1}.
\end{aligned} \tag{5}
\]
Here \(\sigma>0\) follows from the variance-range assumption.  Multiplying \((4)\) by \(\sigma^2\) proves the claimed conditional covariance sandwich.

The causal coefficient remains distinct from its observed-law identifying functional.  Indeed, linear response, iterated expectation, and conditional centering show
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \mathbb E_{d^\star}[x_aY_a]
 &=\mathbb E_{d^\star}[x_ax_a^{\mathsf T}]\beta
   +\mathbb E_{d^\star}[x_a\epsilon_a]\\
 &=\Sigma\beta
   +\mathbb E_{d^\star}\!\left[x_a\mathbb E(\epsilon_a\mid F)\right]
 =\Sigma\beta.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus the invertibility established above proves, rather than defines, the relationship \(\beta=\Sigma^{-1}\mathbb E_{d^\star}[x_aY_a]\).

The event \(G_n(\varepsilon)\) is measurable with respect to \(F\).  On that event, equation \((5)\) and the zero conditional mean imply
\[
 \mathbb E\!\left[\|\widehat\beta_\varepsilon-\beta\|_2^2\mid F\right]
 =\sigma^2\operatorname{tr}\{(F^{\mathsf T}F)^{-1}\}.
\]
On its complement, the estimator definition gives \(\widehat\beta_\varepsilon=0\), so the squared error is exactly \(\|\beta\|_2^2\).  Splitting over the two disjoint events and taking expectations proves
\[
 R_n(\beta,\sigma,\varepsilon)
 =\sigma^2\mathbb E_{d^\star}\!\left[
   \mathbf 1_{G_n(\varepsilon)}
   \operatorname{tr}\{(F^{\mathsf T}F)^{-1}\}\right]
 +\|\beta\|_2^2b_{n,\varepsilon}. \tag{6}
\]
Taking traces in \((4)\), using \(\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma^{-1})=\Phi^\star\), multiplying by \(\mathbf 1_{G_n(\varepsilon)}\), and averaging gives
\[
 \frac{\sigma^2\Phi^\star}{n(1+\varepsilon)}(1-b_{n,\varepsilon})
 \le
 \sigma^2\mathbb E_{d^\star}\!\left[
   \mathbf 1_{G_n(\varepsilon)}
   \operatorname{tr}\{(F^{\mathsf T}F)^{-1}\}\right]
 \le
 \frac{\sigma^2\Phi^\star}{n(1-\varepsilon)}(1-b_{n,\varepsilon}).
\]
For the lower risk bound, add the nonnegative fallback term in \((6)\).  For the upper risk bound, discard the factor \(1-b_{n,\varepsilon}\le1\) and use \(\|\beta\|_2^2\le B^2\).  This yields
\[
 \frac{\sigma^2\Phi^\star}{n}\frac{1-b_{n,\varepsilon}}{1+\varepsilon}
 \le R_n(\beta,\sigma,\varepsilon)
 \le\frac{\sigma^2\Phi^\star}{n(1-\varepsilon)}+B^2b_{n,\varepsilon}.
\]
Finally, \(0<\varepsilon<1/2\) implies \((1-\varepsilon)^{-1}\le1+2\varepsilon\), and the Chernoff bound gives
\[
 B^2b_{n,\varepsilon}
 \le2B^2q\exp\!\left\{-\frac{n\varepsilon^2}{3\mu^\star}\right\}.
\]
Substitution proves
\[
 R_n(\beta,\sigma,\varepsilon)
 \le\frac{\sigma^2\Phi^\star}{n}(1+2\varepsilon)
 +2B^2q\exp\!\left\{-\frac{n\varepsilon^2}{3\mu^\star}\right\}.
\]
Every step uses only the stated first two conditional noise moments; conditional Gaussianity is unnecessary.

By \(\textnormal{ass:fixed-dimension}\), the quantities \(q\), \(\mu^\star\), and \(\Phi^\star\) are fixed as \(n\to\infty\).  The exact leverage formula gives \(0<\mu^\star<\infty\), while the positive definiteness of \(\Sigma_k(d^\star)\) gives \(0<\Phi^\star<\infty\).  Since \(n/\log n\to\infty\), for all sufficiently large \(n\) one has \(n>36\mu^\star\log n\).  Hence \(\textnormal{def:oracle-threshold}\) applies and gives
\[
 \varepsilon_n=3\sqrt{\frac{\mu^\star\log n}{n}},
 \qquad
 0<\varepsilon_n<\frac12,
 \qquad
 \varepsilon_n\longrightarrow0.
\]
The middle inequality follows directly from \(n>36\mu^\star\log n\).

Write \(b_n=b_{n,\varepsilon_n}\).  The concentration conclusion of \(\textnormal{thm:risk-sandwich}\), followed by the definition of \(\varepsilon_n\), yields
\[
 b_n
 \le 2q\exp\!\left\{-\frac{n\varepsilon_n^2}{3\mu^\star}\right\}
 =2q\exp\{-3\log n\}
 =2qn^{-3}. \tag{1}
\]
For every coefficient vector, noise scale, and conditional-noise law in the supremum of the theorem, define
\[
 \rho_n(\beta,\sigma)
 =\frac{R_n(\beta,\sigma,\varepsilon_n)}{\sigma^2\Phi^\star/n}.
\]
This ratio is well defined because \(\sigma\ge\sigma_{\min}>0\) and \(\Phi^\star>0\).  Dividing the two-sided conclusion of \(\textnormal{thm:risk-sandwich}\) by \(\sigma^2\Phi^\star/n\) gives
\[
 \frac{1-b_n}{1+\varepsilon_n}
 \le \rho_n(\beta,\sigma)
 \le \frac{1}{1-\varepsilon_n}
   +\frac{nB^2b_n}{\sigma^2\Phi^\star}. \tag{2}
\]
The deficit of the left endpoint in \((2)\) from one satisfies
\[
 1-\frac{1-b_n}{1+\varepsilon_n}
 =\frac{\varepsilon_n+b_n}{1+\varepsilon_n}
 \le \varepsilon_n+b_n, \tag{3}
\]
whereas, because \(0<\varepsilon_n<1/2\), the excess of the right endpoint over one satisfies
\[
 \frac{1}{1-\varepsilon_n}-1
   +\frac{nB^2b_n}{\sigma^2\Phi^\star}
 \le 2\varepsilon_n
   +\frac{nB^2b_n}{\sigma^2\Phi^\star}. \tag{4}
\]
Equations \((1)\)--\((4)\) and \(\sigma^2\ge\sigma_{\min}^2\) imply, simultaneously for every element of the stated parameter and conditional-noise class,
\[
 \left|\rho_n(\beta,\sigma)-1\right|
 \le
 2\varepsilon_n+2qn^{-3}
 +\frac{2B^2q}{\sigma_{\min}^2\Phi^\star}n^{-2}. \tag{5}
\]
The right-hand side of \((5)\) is deterministic, independent of \(\beta\), \(\sigma\), and the admissible conditional-noise law, and converges to zero.  Taking the required supremum proves the asserted uniform convergence.  The proof keeps \(p,k,L,B,\sigma_{\min},\sigma_{\max}\) fixed and therefore makes no growing-dimensional or vanishing-supply uniformity claim.
